summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in cipher feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option, defining two key sizes.

eli5.summary: This picks the CAST-128 scrambler, used in another way, for hiding Telnet text, with two key sizes.

subtitle: Uses CAST-128 encryption in cipher feedback mode to secure Telnet

tldr.problem: Telnet sends passwords and commands in plain text, exposing them to eavesdropping and active attacks on insecure networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to use the CAST-128 cipher algorithm in 64-bit cipher feedback mode (CFB64) during Telnet sessions, supporting both 40-bit and 128-bit key sizes for encryption negotiation.
tldr.outcome: Telnet sessions can negotiate encryption using cipher feedback mode, which offers better protection against active text substitution attacks than output feedback mode.

today: RFC 2950 is a Proposed Standard specifying CAST-128 cipher feedback mode encryption for Telnet. It remains published but is largely superseded in practice by SSH and other modern secure remote access protocols.

sections.title: Cipher Feedback Mode for Telnet
sections.content:
Telnet transmits all session data in plain text, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping. The Telnet encryption option provides a negotiation mechanism to enable encryption during Telnet sessions.

This RFC specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in 64-bit cipher feedback mode (CFB64) with the Telnet encryption option. Two key sizes are defined: 40-bit (CAST5_40_CFB64, type 8) and 128-bit (CAST128_CFB64, type 10) encryption keys.
sections.eli5: Like the output feedback version, this scrambles Telnet text, but it does so in a way that makes it harder for attackers to trick the connection.

sections.title: Cipher Feedback Algorithm
sections.content:
Cipher feedback mode is a streaming encryption mode where the previous ciphertext block feeds back into the cipher to generate the next keystream block. This feedback from the encrypted data creates dependency between blocks, making the cipher more resistant to active attacks than output feedback mode.

Both parties negotiate an 8-byte initial vector using the CFB64_IV command. Once an IV_OK response is received, key negotiation proceeds using ENC_KEYID. After a common key is identified, START and END commands enable and disable encryption. If encryption is toggled off and back on with the same key, the intermediate clear text must not change the state of the encryption machine.
sections.eli5: The cipher creates bits to mix with the text, but the bits depend on the previous encrypted output, making patterns harder to predict and harder to manipulate.

sections.title: Security Characteristics
sections.content:
Cipher feedback mode does not ensure data integrity, but it offers limited protection against active text substitution. An active attacker can modify a maximum of 8 bytes at a time; the following 8-byte block of data will be corrupted, making detection likely. However, this is not a complete guarantee against exploitation.

The 40-bit key mode is not considered secure and is listed only to document implementations already prevalent on the Internet. Adding a message authentication code (MAC) would significantly increase overhead for Telnet, which is why it is not used here.
sections.eli5: An attacker could still change some data, but it would corrupt the next part and be detectable. The 40-bit version is weak and only used with old systems.

references.text: Adams, C., "The CAST-128 Encryption Algorithm", RFC 2144, May 1997.
